title: Greetings & Basics
pronunciation_focus_summary: Nasal vowels — the sounds that make French sound French. Found in bonjour, bien, bon, and dozens of common words. Learn to let air flow through your nose while shaping vowels with your mouth.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'on' is a nasal vowel — say 'on' but let air flow through your nose. The 'j' sounds like 'zh' (like the 's' in 'measure'). The final 'r' is the soft French R, produced in the back of the throat.
Same nasal 'on' as bonjour. The 'soir' contains the 'wa' sound — round your lips. The final 'r' is the soft uvular R.
phrases.example_sentence: Bonsoir, une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The final 't' is silent. The 'u' is the French U sound — purse your lips tightly and say 'ee'. It is NOT the English 'oo' sound.
Two uvular R sounds here. The 'au' sounds like 'oh'. The 'oi' makes the 'wa' sound. Let the R's be soft and throaty.
Three words that flow together as one. The final 't' is silent. The 'ê' in 'plaît' makes an open 'eh' sound (like 'bed').
The 'er' makes an open 'eh' sound, not 'ur'. The 'r' is the soft French R. Stress falls on the second syllable.
The 'eau' in beaucoup makes an 'oh' sound. The final 'p' is silent. The 'ou' is a simple 'oo' sound — different from the French U.
The 'e' in 'de' is a schwa — a quick, neutral 'uh'. The 'ien' is a nasal vowel: say 'ee-eh' but nasalize it. Don't pronounce the final 'n'.
The 'u' in 'excusez' is the French U (lips pursed, tongue forward). The 'ez' ending sounds like 'ay'. The 'moi' sounds like 'mwa'.
The 'on' is the nasal vowel — air through the nose, don't pronounce the 'n'. The 'r' is the uvular R. Stress is on the second syllable.
Simple and short. Sounds like English 'we'. Keep it crisp — one syllable.
This is a nasal vowel. The 'n' at the end is NOT pronounced as a consonant — instead it nasalizes the 'o'. Push air through your nose while saying 'no'.
The 'omm' creates a nasal 'oh' sound. 'ent' at the end of 'comment' is silent. The 't' of 'comment' links to 'allez' in liaison. The 'ez' sounds like 'ay'.
The 'è' in 'très' is an open 'eh'. The 'ien' in 'bien' is a nasal vowel — nasalize the 'ee-eh' sound. The 's' of 'très' links to 'bien' in liaison: 'treh-ZBYEHN'.
Two nasal vowels: 'om' in comprends and 'an' at the end. The 'ds' is silent. The 'j' makes the 'zh' sound. In casual speech, the 'ne' is often dropped: 'je comprends pas'.
phrases.example_sentence: Désolé, je ne comprends pas. Pouvez-vous répéter ?

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.translation: Very well, thank you. And you?

dialogues.notes: Use 'vous' (formal you) with people you just met or in professional situations. This is the safe default.

dialogues.context: Asking for help on the street

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Pardon, je ne comprends pas. Vous parlez anglais ?
exchanges.translation: Sorry, I don't understand. Do you speak English?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: pahr-DOHN zhuh nuh kohn-PRAHN PAH. voo pahr-LAY ahn-GLEH?

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.text: Un peu. Je peux vous aider.
exchanges.translation: A little. I can help you.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: uhn PUH. zhuh PUH vooz ay-DAY.

dialogues.notes: Starting with 'excusez-moi' or 'pardon' is considered polite when approaching a stranger in France. Always greet before asking for help.
French people almost always add a pleasantry when saying goodbye: 'bonne journée' (have a good day), 'bonne soirée' (have a good evening), or 'à bientôt' (see you soon).

cultural_notes.title: La bise — the cheek kiss greeting
cultural_notes.content: In France, friends and acquaintances greet each other with 'la bise' — light kisses on alternating cheeks. The number varies by region (1-4), but 2 is most common in Paris. In professional settings, a handshake is standard. When in doubt, follow the other person's lead. Since COVID, la bise has become less automatic — many people now prefer a wave or elbow bump.

cultural_notes.title: Always say Bonjour first
cultural_notes.content: In France, greeting someone before any interaction is essential. When entering a shop, say 'Bonjour'. When approaching a stranger for directions, start with 'Bonjour' or 'Excusez-moi'. Skipping the greeting and going straight to a request is considered rude. Think of 'Bonjour' as opening a social door — without it, the conversation starts on the wrong foot.
